extracted.intended_audience: painters, sculptors, architects, art students, connoisseurs, and patrons (readers interested in the theory and practice of the fine arts)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes Vasari's Preface criteria for what constitutes excellent painting, sculpture, and architecture — including technical knowledge, judgement, materials, and the virtues of practice and design. Useful for assessing or producing works in the Renaissance fine-arts tradition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design (disegno) as foundation
rubrics_metrics.description: “design, which is their foundation, nay rather, the very soul that conceives and nourishes within itself all the parts of man's intellect” — design is the fundamental principle from which painting and sculpture arise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both painting and sculpture are born from design; mastery of disegno is the primary requirement for excellence in either art and is treated as their common source and guiding principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nobility judged by letters, practice, excellence, and judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Art’s nobility must be derived from “letters, of practice, of excellence, and of judgment” rather than from material durability, riches, mythic anecdotes, or popular adoration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assess an art’s worth by the longevity of its materials (e.g., marble) or by stories of patronage — evaluate on intellectual learning, technical practice, excellence of execution, and sound judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breadth of painting's branches and their value
rubrics_metrics.description: Painting embraces many subordinate arts: invention of history, foreshortening, branches of architecture for building-making, perspective, distemper colouring, fresco, oils (on wood/stone/canvas), illumination, stained glass, mosaics, inlay, sgraffito, niello, copper printing, enamelling, damascening, glazed figure-painting, pottery painting, weaving (brocades, tapestry), etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competence across these varied branches increases a painter’s usefulness and the art’s claim to superiority; painting’s multiplicity of applications is cited as evidence of its scope and utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sculptor's need for absolute and immediate perfection of judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Sculptors allegedly require “a perfection of judgment... absolute and immediate, in a manner that it may see within the marble the exact whole of that figure” because carving removes material irreversibly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sculptural work demands decisive pre-vision and planning since errors are often irreparable; this criterion emphasizes the necessity of seeing the finished figure within the block before chiselling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reparability of medium affects required technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Painters can correct slips with the brush, covering and patching errors; sculptors cannot so easily remedy mistakes in stone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating technique or assigning difficulty, consider whether the medium permits correction — media that allow corrections (painting) afford iterative work and different working practices than irreversible media (stone carving).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice and access to materials required for mastery
rubrics_metrics.description: Mastery depends on opportunity to practice: “he who cannot use and waste a small quantity of marble...cannot have that practice...he who does not practise does not learn it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessors should factor in whether an artist had resources/time to practice; scarcity of materials (e.g., marble) and lack of patronage limit technical development and number of competent practitioners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental study vs. bodily labour: value of intellectual knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: “The true difficulties lie rather in the mind than in the body... painters rely more on the worth of the mind” — intellectual study (geometry, perspective, physiognomy) is presented as a higher difficulty than mere physical toil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give weight to cognitive/learned aspects of an artist’s competence (study of perspective, anatomy, composition) when judging nobility or merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical knowledge required for painting (perspective, foreshortening, architecture)
rubrics_metrics.description: Painters must know perspective, the invention of history scenes, the most difficult art of foreshortening, branches of architecture, and many other technical matters beyond simply landscape and buildings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess painting by the artist's command of perspective, foreshortening, and architectural representation when present in compositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge of colours and representation of transparent/intangible forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Painters must “know the forms not only of all the bodies supported and not supported, but also of all those transparent and intangible; and besides this they must know the colours that are suitable for the said bodies.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate a painter’s sensitivity to colour, translucency, and subtle material properties (e.g., glass, water, breath) as a mark of technical and perceptual mastery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depicting emotions, motion, and physiognomy
rubrics_metrics.description: Painters can express “all the forms of motion... even with breath itself and the spiritual essence of sight” and must understand physiognomy to depict passions and events convincingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judgement of figural work should attend to the convincing rendering of emotion, motion, facial expression, and subtle gestures — areas where painting is argued to excel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of models, instruments, and patience to prevent mistakes
rubrics_metrics.description: Painters use models, protractors, squares, compasses, and devices for enlarging; patience and tools “not only preserves them from mistakes but enables them to bring their whole work to its perfection.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess technical rigor by the use of preparatory models, measurements, and instruments; patience and methodical technique are positive indicators of quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fresco-specific demands (speed, foresight, irreversibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fresco work permits no patience or time: the artist must foresee the end in the fresh plaster and complete areas in one day; retouches on dry plaster are disdained and liable to mould and loss on washing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate fresco by the artist’s compositional foresight, decisiveness, and ability to execute complex passages within the fresh-plaster time window; detect retouching or unstable repairs as faults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplicity and compositional variety in painting
rubrics_metrics.description: Painters can place many figures on a single panel with varied postures, foreshortenings, and attitudes, and can represent multiple aspects/views of a figure in one painting (e.g., use of mirrors, pools).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess compositional complexity and the successful integration of many figures or multiple viewpoints as indicators of painterly skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Painting's capacity to render elements and nature fully
rubrics_metrics.description: Painting adorns the air, water, earth, and fire with their varieties (light/darkness, birds, fish, plants, buildings, flames) and renders nature’s multiplicity and true colours so that nature itself marvels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value the work for fidelity and richness in rendering natural phenomena and elemental effects; consider breadth and subtlety of environmental depiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sculpture’s limits in emotional representation and viewing
rubrics_metrics.description: Sculpture is said to represent emotions less fully (limited to motion and limb shapes) and to be viewed from many sides, whereas painting supplies infinite forms of motion and subtlety for the viewer's single-sided perspective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating sculpture, consider both the three-dimensional viewing advantage and the medium’s relative constraints in expressing inner passions; judge success by how well the sculptor overcomes those constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patience as the chief quality transferring model to marble
rubrics_metrics.description: “The quality that little by little transfers their models to the marble is rather patience than aught else.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For sculpture, assess patience and stepwise method (working from models) more than speed; methodical transfer from model to stone indicates good practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architecture judged by universality, necessity, and proportions
rubrics_metrics.description: Architecture is the most universal and necessary art; evaluation requires understanding varieties of stone, methods of construction, and their proportions so one may “recognize buildings that are good and well-conceived.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess buildings by material use, construction methods, and especially proportion and conception; architecture’s service and ornament function should be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for good sculpture: form and proportion
rubrics_metrics.description: Good sculpture is identified by how statues are wrought, “the form and the proportion that are looked for in them,” and adherence to secret and necessary precepts of the craft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge sculpture on anatomical/formal correctness and proportion, and on observance of established sculptural precepts and methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for good painting: draughtsmanship, colouring, execution quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Good painting requires draughtsmanship, methods of colouring, and “the perfect execution of any work, of the quality of the pictures themselves,” and mastery across related arts (mosaic, niello, enamelling, damascening, printing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate painting primarily on drawing/draftsmanship, colour handling, execution quality, and competence in relevant techniques and media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of historical knowledge and artists' biographies
rubrics_metrics.description: Reading the history and Lives of craftsmen teaches where works are, how to recognize their perfection or imperfection, and how to discriminate between manners — producing delight and practical instruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use historical examples and biographical study as part of evaluation and training: comparative history is a practical guide to recognizing excellence and learning from past accidents and virtues.
